bib.venue: Packt (book chapter); authors and year are not printed in the chapter PDF

read.by: main-session (source-reader dispatch refused: concurrent subagent limit)

question: What distinguishes an agent from an LLM or a workflow, what are its components, and how do agents communicate with each other and with tools?
contributions: LLM versus automated workflow versus agent comparison (Table 4.1)
Seven-part agent anatomy: goals, sense, reason, plan, act, memory, coordinate (Table 4.2)
Travel planning and loan processing case studies
Three-layer stack: function calling, tool protocols, agent-to-agent protocols

results.claim: An MMM is not an agent: the model is stateless and passive, responds only when prompted, and does not pursue goals on its own.
results.quote: However, an MMM is not an agent.

results.claim: An automated workflow follows a fixed path and cannot reason, plan dynamically or adapt to unforeseen circumstances.
results.setup: Definitional contrast with agents (Table 4.1); no measurement.
results.quote: deterministic and rigid, following a fixed path.

results.claim: The Coordinate component tracks agent-to-agent task states such as submitted, working, input-required and completed.
results.setup: Design description of A2A; no interoperability test.

results.claim: Direct communication is an explicit message from one agent to another; indirect communication (stigmergy) is observing and modifying a shared environment such as a database.
results.setup: Supply-chain examples (reorder_part message; status complete record); no measurement.
results.quote: Indirect communication (Stigmergy): Agents can also interact indirectly by observing

results.claim: Sending tasks directly to the Risk Agent and then the Approval Agent, with the score in the payload, creates a clear, auditable chain of delegation.
results.quote: This creates a clear, auditable chain of delegation.

results.claim: Tool protocols such as MCP decouple tool hosting from the agent, so tools become portable services like REST APIs.
results.setup: Qualitative comparison with framework-bound tool executors.
results.quote: effectively turning tools into portable services much like REST APIs.

results.claim: Many sophisticated systems use a hybrid: function calling for internal actions and higher-level protocols for external collaboration.

limits: No measured results; all scenarios (travel, loan, supply chain) are illustrative.
The agent versus workflow table is a definitional contrast, not an empirical comparison.
Physical sensors and actuators are covered only by example.
practices: Separate the reasoning model from the agent structure that supplies goals, memory and tools.
Use direct messages for auditable delegation and a shared record for loose coupling.
Use function calling inside one runtime, MCP across tool boundaries, A2A across agent boundaries.

terms.definition: Indirect coordination through observing and modifying a shared environment.
Metadata advertising what a remote agent can do (from ch. 1).
